solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Go westwards over motorway, having walked (7)

indicators.note: in an across clue, going west means reading right to left
the reversed word goes over, i.e. around, the motorway

blocks.note: to go = to depart
M = motorway, as in the M1

annotation.surface: A driver gives up on the road and heads off on foot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Over' reads as crossing a bridge above the road, but here it means the reversed word straddles the motorway letter.
annotation.definitionFit: To tramp is to walk heavily or over a long distance, so the past tense fits 'walked' in a sentence.

clue.text: Film, one that went down, in the main, rather dreadfully? (7)

definitions.text: one that went down, in the main, rather dreadfully

blocks.note: a 1997 James Cameron blockbuster

blocks.clueFragment: one that went down, in the main, rather dreadfully
blocks.note: a liner lost in the Atlantic in 1912; the main is the open sea

annotation.surface: A dig at a film that sank rather badly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Main' is an old word for the sea. The question mark covers the joke that the film, not only the ship, might be said to have gone down dreadfully.
annotation.definitionFit: Titanic is both the title of the film and the name of the ship whose sinking it dramatises.

clue.text: Sun, Daily Star etc put out work of fiction (1,5,2,7)

indicators.note: letters put out of order are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 15 letters

annotation.surface: Tabloid newspapers publishing something made up.
annotation.walkthrough: The Sun and the Daily Star are British tabloids, so the surface sneers that they print fiction; 'put out' seems to mean publish but scrambles the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A Study in Scarlet, Arthur Conan Doyle's 1887 novel introducing Sherlock Holmes, is a work of fiction by example.

clue.text: Urge American to visit British drinking establishment (4)

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside the place visited

blocks.note: PH = public house, as on British maps
US = American

annotation.surface: Encouraging a US tourist to try a British pub.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the front and reads as the verb of the sentence, which hides it well.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to urge someone on is to press or drive them forward.

clue.text: Men travelling in Black Country (7)

indicators.note: letters on the move are rearranged
the rearranged letters go inside the other word

blocks.note: black = dark
MEN rearranged

annotation.surface: Men journeying through the Black Country, the industrial West Midlands of England.
annotation.walkthrough: The Black Country is an English region, which tempts you to read 'Black Country' as one phrase; 'Country' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: Denmark is a Scandinavian nation, so 'country' names the class it belongs to.

clue.text: Upper-class bishop leaves rum cocktail measure (7)

indicators.note: the letters leave, so they are removed

blocks.note: a Cuba libre is rum and cola
U = upper-class, removed
B = bishop in chess notation, removed

annotation.surface: A posh bishop walks away from his drink.
annotation.walkthrough: Only the first B goes; the second stays in LIBRE. 'Leaves' tempts you to read foliage or departure, not removal.
annotation.definitionFit: Calibre is the measured bore of a gun barrel, and figuratively the measure of a person's quality.

clue.text: Work from Potter after getting fired? (7)

definitions.text: Work from Potter after getting fired?

blocks.note: the capital P suggests an author such as Beatrix Potter; really it is any potter at the wheel
not sacked from a job but baked in a kiln

annotation.surface: A writer called Potter loses a job and turns out new work.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves carry a second sense: Potter the author becomes a craftsman, and being fired becomes kiln-baking, which is what turns clay into a ceramic.
annotation.definitionFit: A ceramic is an object of clay hardened by firing, exactly the finished work of a potter.

clue.text: Left at home finally gutting fish (4)

indicators.note: take the final letter of the next word

blocks.note: L = left
in = at home
last letter of gutting

annotation.surface: Someone left at home to finish cleaning the fish.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gutting fish' reads as one kitchen phrase, but 'fish' is the definition standing alone at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the ling is a long, cod-like North Atlantic sea fish.

clue.text: Notes produced by the Speaker for the lobby? (10,5)

definitions.text: Notes produced by the Speaker for the lobby?

blocks.note: suggests memos from the Speaker of the House of Commons; really musical notes from a loudspeaker
not the parliamentary lobby but a hotel or office foyer

annotation.surface: The Speaker of the House of Commons issuing notes for parliamentary lobbyists.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital S and 'lobby' conjure Westminster; switch to a loudspeaker in a hotel foyer and the notes become music nobody is meant to listen to closely.
annotation.definitionFit: Background music is the unobtrusive music piped through speakers into public spaces such as foyers.

clue.text: Oriental religious festival ending in afternoon (7)

indicators.note: take the ending, the last letter, of the next word

blocks.note: the Christian festival of the Resurrection
last letter of afternoon

annotation.surface: An Eastern religious festival that runs until the afternoon.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Oriental religious festival' reads as one phrase, pointing to something like Diwali; 'Oriental' is the definition on its own.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: oriental literally means of the east, from Latin oriens, the rising sun.

clue.text: Studio curtains ordered, hosting new RSC production (5,10)

indicators.note: letters put in order are rearranged
the fodder takes in an extra letter

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters
N = new, added to the fodder

annotation.surface: A theatre orders new curtains for a Royal Shakespeare Company show.
annotation.walkthrough: The RSC is the Royal Shakespeare Company, so the production is a Shakespeare play; 'ordered' reads as buying curtains, not rearranging them.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Titus Andronicus is Shakespeare's bloodiest tragedy, part of the RSC repertoire.

clue.text: Finale of Byron poem that might bring a lump to the throat? (4)

indicators.note: take the finale, the last letter, of the next word

blocks.note: last letter of Byron
an ode is a lyric poem
surface padding describing the poem's effect
surface padding completing 'a lump in the throat'

annotation.surface: The end of a Byron poem moves the reader to tears.
annotation.walkthrough: A lump in the throat is emotion, but the definition is a physical lump; the swollen glands felt in the neck are lymph nodes, so the tail still fits.
annotation.definitionFit: A node is a small swelling or knot in tissue, a lump in medical terms.

clue.text: Crazy pub, goodness! (5)

blocks.note: a bar = a pub
my! = goodness!, an exclamation of surprise

annotation.surface: Someone exclaiming at a wild pub.
annotation.walkthrough: The exclamation 'goodness!' can be swapped for the one-word gasp 'my!', which is easy to overlook as a letter source.
annotation.definitionFit: Regional use: barmy is British slang for mad, originally frothing like barm, the yeast on beer.

clue.text: Giant conger-eel regularly sliced (4)

indicators.note: cutting at regular intervals keeps every other letter

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

annotation.surface: A huge conger eel cut into regular steaks.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Giant' reads as an adjective describing the eel, but it is the noun definition.
annotation.definitionFit: An ogre is a man-eating giant of folklore, so the noun 'giant' covers it.

clue.text: Doctor set up appropriate theme (5)

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means written bottom to top

blocks.note: MO = medical officer
fit = appropriate

annotation.surface: A doctor chooses a fitting theme.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Set up' looks as if it goes with Doctor, but it only turns the second word upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A motif is a recurring idea or pattern in art, music or writing, which is a theme.

clue.text: Holiday snap (5)

blocks.note: a short trip away, as in a city weekend
as a verb: to crack in two

annotation.surface: A holiday photo.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Holiday snap' reads as a photograph; split it into two separate definitions, and read snap as a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: the noun is a short getaway such as a city weekend, and the verb means to crack something in two.

clue.text: Native American agreed to put on cotton cloth (7)

blocks.note: chino is a twilled cotton cloth
OK = agreed

annotation.surface: Someone agrees to wear cotton clothing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Put on' suggests getting dressed; in an across clue it means one piece is attached after the other.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Chinook are a Native American people of the Pacific Northwest.

clue.text: Daffy actor playing Mickey Mouse? (7)

indicators.note: daffy means crazy, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: ACTOR rearranged
on = playing, as in a show that is on

annotation.surface: Daffy Duck as an actor playing Mickey Mouse.
annotation.walkthrough: Daffy suggests Daffy Duck, which fits the animated theme but is the anagram indicator. The question mark flags Mickey Mouse as one example.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Mickey Mouse is a Disney animated character, the star of a cartoon.

clue.text: Terminate bank clerk (7)

blocks.note: as a verb: to dismiss from service, especially from the armed forces
the person behind the counter handling money

annotation.surface: An order to fire a bank employee.
annotation.walkthrough: The verb sense, to dismiss in disgrace, is chiefly military and less familiar than the bank job.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: the verb means to sack someone, and the noun is a bank or shop clerk who handles cash.

clue.text: California agent rejected old West Indian song (7)

indicators.note: thrown back, so written backwards

blocks.note: Cal. = California
a spy is a secret agent
O = old

annotation.surface: A Californian talent agent turns down an old Caribbean song.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface agent is a Hollywood talent agent; the setter means a secret agent.
annotation.definitionFit: Calypso is the song style of Trinidad, sung in the Caribbean islands long called the West Indies.

clue.text: End in torn clothing (7)

indicators.note: one word goes inside the other

blocks.note: rent = torn
an end is an aim or goal

annotation.surface: Finishing up in ripped clothes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'End' looks like a last-letter signal, but here it means a goal; rent is the old past participle of rend.
annotation.definitionFit: Archaic use: raiment is a literary word for garments, surviving mostly in biblical language.

clue.text: Surrey town‘s blemishes reported (7)

indicators.note: what is reported is heard, so go by sound

blocks.note: stains are blemishes

annotation.surface: Blemishes are reported in a Surrey town.
annotation.walkthrough: Surrey is a county just south-west of London.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Staines-upon-Thames, near Heathrow, is one of Surrey's towns.

clue.text: Tesco use recycled bags one found in Liverpool (7)

indicators.note: the phrase holds the answer, like a bag

blocks.note: teSCO USE Recycled

annotation.surface: Tesco reusing its shopping bags in a Liverpool store.
annotation.walkthrough: Tesco is a British supermarket chain. 'Recycled' looks like an anagram signal but only lends its first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Regional use: Scouse is the Liverpool dialect and stew, so a Liverpudlian is known as a Scouser.

clue.text: Exercise leg and bottom? (3-4)

blocks.note: an abdominal exercise lifting the torso from lying
in cricket the leg side is also called the on side

annotation.surface: A workout for legs and buttocks.
annotation.walkthrough: In cricket, leg and on both name the half of the field behind the batter's legs. The question mark marks a jokey word for the bottom.
annotation.definitionFit: Idiom: sit-upon is a humorous British word for the buttocks, literally the part you sit on.

clue.text: Burden ordinary youngster carries (4)

indicators.note: the carrier holds the other letters inside

blocks.note: a lad is a youngster
O = ordinary, as in the old O level exam

annotation.surface: An ordinary child carries a heavy burden.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Burden' reads as a verb in the surface, but works as a noun definition too.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a load is something heavy that must be carried, a burden.

clue.text: Disgraced president naked? (5)

blocks.note: the US leader who resigned over Watergate in 1974
wearing nothing, split as slang for nothing plus 'on'

annotation.surface: Asking whether a disgraced president was caught without clothes.
annotation.walkthrough: Nix is slang for nothing, so NIX ON is nothing on; the question mark admits the pun.
annotation.definitionFit: Richard Nixon resigned in disgrace, and split in two his name reads as having nothing on.

clue.text: Skip – very clever dog – denied good run (4)

indicators.note: the word is denied the letters, so they are taken away

blocks.note: Gromit, the brainy dog of Wallace and Gromit
G = good, removed
R = run in cricket scores, removed

annotation.surface: A clever dog called Skip is kept from a good run.
annotation.walkthrough: Wallace and Gromit are British clay-animation characters; Gromit is the silent, far cleverer dog. 'Skip' looks like the dog's name.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to skip a step is to leave it out.

clue.text: Engine Charlie parked in station, out of Water? (4)

indicators.note: the letter is parked inside the other word
take the station with 'Water' out

blocks.note: Waterloo station without WATER
C = Charlie in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: An engine parked at a station has run out of water.
annotation.walkthrough: Waterloo is a London railway station; the capital W hints that 'Water' names part of a word, not a steam engine's supply.
annotation.definitionFit: Loco is the railway shortening of locomotive, the engine that pulls a train.

clue.text: Taxi carrying southern strikebreaker (4)

indicators.note: the carrier holds the other letter

blocks.note: a cab is a taxi
S = southern

annotation.surface: A taxi driving a strikebreaker through the picket line.
annotation.walkthrough: The carried letter sits at the very front, so the container holds it only at the edge.
annotation.definitionFit: Slang: a scab is a worker who crosses a picket line during a strike.

clue.text: Klopp counsels us to work, work harder (4,4,5,2)

blocks.note: a football manager telling players to get kitted out for the match
the idiom for making more effort

annotation.surface: Jürgen Klopp urging his team to try harder.
annotation.walkthrough: Jürgen Klopp managed Liverpool FC; for footballers, hauling up long socks is literally part of getting ready to play.
annotation.definitionFit: Idiom: to pull one's socks up is to make more effort, and for a footballer it is also literal kit.

clue.text: Dismissed job in far-flung location (7)

blocks.note: a batter dismissed in cricket is out
a post is a job

annotation.surface: Someone sacked and sent to a remote post.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container signal; it only joins wordplay to definition.
annotation.definitionFit: An outpost is a remote settlement or military station far from the centre.

clue.text: Massage revered figure after which there’s no going back (7)

definitions.text: after which there’s no going back

blocks.note: a rub is a massage
an icon is a revered figure

annotation.surface: A massage for a celebrity that proves irreversible.
annotation.walkthrough: Caesar crossing the river Rubicon in 49 BC made civil war inevitable; 'after' looks like a placement instruction but belongs to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Allusion: crossing the Rubicon means passing a point of no return, a line after which there is no going back.
